# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–22 (Complete – Updated 162)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of sixth year** (Chapter 22). George has departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne; Amelia now walks to Russell Square evenings when George does not visit, resting by garden railing, praying as lights go out in his chamber. Little Rawdon sent to school; Rawdon visited him shortly after and found him well and happy.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opens "It was the summer of the sixth year." Jos's annuity still paying despite Old Sedley's deception. Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year (Chapter 21) completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph. Great George on throne; ladies wore gigots and tortoise-shell combs. Later seasonal details: Rain threatened since morning but held off; bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs; bees hum in lavender behind parsonage; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; children chased hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw. Frost silvered hedges overnight.
- **Locations**: Salwick; Harrowgate; Dunholt; Bryngate (Tassa Brackwood departed); Yarlton (Tassa settled; Colan Lindson followed within month); London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street, Russell Square, Baker Street, Hyde Park Ring, Levant House, Foundling Church, Gaunt House, Gaunt Square, Serpentine, Cursitor Street); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gulton; Mirecombe; Brookgreen Fair; Coldcombe; Fenmere; school in City; Astley's; May Fair; Chancery Lane; the Temple; Paddington.

## Rebecca's Ascendant Period and Deterioration (Chapters 21–22)

**Social Triumphs**: Court presentation, Gaunt House musical triumph, diplomatic circles including French Embassy and Prince of Peterwaradin, exclusive supper placement, elaborate charades entertainment.

**Contempt for Rawdon and Growing Isolation**: Dismisses him patronizingly: "Do what you like--dine where you please--go and have ginger-beer and sawdust at Astley's, or psalm-singing with Lady Jane--only don't expect me to busy myself with the boy." Claims credit for his social position. Nobody wants Rawdon at parties; she is often asked without him. Looks upon him as errand-man and humble slave, did not care or miss him or anybody.

**Steyne's Financial Schemes and Investigations (Chapter 22)**
- Previously gave Becky money to pay off debt to Briggs; suspected she misappropriated funds but too delicate to confront her.
- **Investigation of Briggs**: Steyne orchestrated "pumping" of Miss Briggs through Mr. Fiche. Extracted truth: Briggs received only black silk gown, nothing else.
- **Truth of Situation**: Rebecca told Steyne false narrative claiming she paid Briggs £1,125. Steyne laughed privately, suspected her scheming, made no additional proposals.
- **Briggs's Actual Position**: Left legacy by Miss Crawley; relatives took part; Colonel invested £600+ with "best security and interest"; Sir Pitt promised to invest remainder. Briggs begged Steyne never tell Rawdon of her confessions.
- **Steyne's Offer to Briggs**: Offered her position at his Hall; Briggs stipulated only that little Rawdon visit her there. Rebecca promised anything and joyfully reported to Rawdon.

**Emerging Concerns About Rebecca's Conduct**
- **Rawdon's Observation**: Told young Southdown of Steyne's bounty; Southdown eyed Crawley with surprising air.
- **Lady Jane and Sir Pitt's Alarm**: Both looked "odd and alarmed." Insisted Rawdon must accompany her everywhere; suggested placing Queen's Crawley girl with her as companion.
- **Sir Pitt's Direct Confrontation**: Expostulated with Rebecca about dismissal of Briggs and receiving young Frenchmen (Messieurs de Truffigny and Champignac), Lord Steyne (whose carriage always at her door, passed hours daily in her company). Implored her to be prudent; society already speaking lightly of her. Expressed indignation at Steyne's attentions, which would compromise any woman.
- **Becky's Promises and Steyne's Continued Visits**: Becky promised anything; but Steyne came to her house as often as ever, and Pitt's anger increased.
- **Lady Jane's Response**: Ambiguous reaction. For refusing all further intercourse with Steyne and declining charades invitation; but Pitt thought acceptance necessary as Royal Highness would attend. At charades party, both Pitts quit early. Becky hardly spoke to Pitt or noticed Lady Jane. Pitt declared her behaviour monstrously indecorous, reprobated play-acting as highly unbecoming a British female, and after charades took brother Rawdon severely to task for appearing and allowing his wife to join in such improper exhibitions.

**Rebecca's Recent Letter to Rawdon (Chapter 22)**
- Beautiful letter on pink paper with light green seal, highly scented.
- Claims she could not sleep, sent for Mr. Blench (doctor) who gave composing draught; ordered Finette not to disturb her.
- Visited Nathan, wept and cried at his knees; he refused to release Rawdon without all money or keeping him in prison.
- Found Lord Steyne ("Milor") at her house with "Bulgarian old sheep-faced monster" offering compliments on last night's performances. Paddington, Champignac, and others came with compliments, plaguing her while she thought of "mon pauvre prisonnier."
- After guests departed, went on knees to Steyne, begged and prayed for two hundred pounds. He refused to let her pawn anything, promised to send money in morning.
- **PLAN, CLAIM**: Steyne promised to send money in morning.
- **CLAIM**: She cared and was distressed; longs to free him.

**Rawdon's Suspicions (Chapter 22)**
- Upon reading Rebecca's letter, Rawdon turned red and looked savage.
- All his suppressed suspicions returned: "She could not even go out and sell her trinkets to free him. She could laugh and talk about compliments paid to her, whilst he was in prison."
- Questions: Who had put him there? Wenham had walked with him. "Was there.... He could hardly bear to think of what he suspected."
- **Unspoken suspicion**: Implied sexual impropriety or conspiracy involving Steyne and possibly Wenham.

## Amelia's Separation and Maternal Anguish (Chapter 22)

**George's Permanent Separation**: Departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne, summer of sixth year. Child elated; mother's heart breaking. Now visits on pony with coachman. Completely unaffected by separation; adopted "slightly imperious air and patronizing manner" within two days. **"He is not her boy any more."** Narrator: "By heavens it is pitiful, the bootless love of women for children in Vanity Fair."

**Daily Ritual of Longing**: On evenings when George does not come, takes long walk to Russell Square; rests by garden railing opposite Osborne house. Looks up at illuminated drawing-room windows; at nine o'clock sees chamber where Georgy sleeps. Prays with humble heart as light goes out; walks home "shrinking and silent," very tired.

**Church Encounter**: One Sunday, saw George and Miss Osborne leaving for church. Little sweep asked charity; Georgy stopped and gave money. Amelia ran round square, gave her mite, followed to Foundling Church where she sat to see boy's head. George's soul thrilled with delight; Amelia's eyes dimmed with tears.

**Physical Decline**: Grows care-worn and sad. Starts up at night, peeps into his room stealthily. Sleeps little. Weeps and prays in long silent nights. Kissed father, placed bill for hundred pounds in his hands before departure.

**Letter to Jos (Chapter 21)**: Wrote tender supplication to Calcutta imploring him not to withdraw support from parents (unaware Jos's annuity continues but money-lender receives it; Sedley sold it for capital).

## Little Rawdon at School (Chapter 22)

**Departure**: Honest Briggs made up little kit. Rebecca would not let Rawdon have carriage; cab brought instead. Rebecca did not offer kiss when he left; child did not propose to embrace her. Walked home very dismally; dined alone with Briggs. Very kind to her, grateful for love and watchfulness. Conscience smote him about borrowing Briggs's money and aiding deception.

**Boy's School Experience**: Young Blackball constituted little Rawdon his fag, shoe-black, and breakfast toaster; initiated him into Latin Grammar; thrashed him three or four times, not severely. Got beating deemed good for him; blacking shoes, toasting bread, fagging deemed necessary parts of young English gentleman's education.

**Rawdon's Visit**: Found lad sufficiently well and happy, grinning and laughing in little black gown and breeches.

## Rawdon's Financial Crisis and Spunging-House (Chapter 22)

**Arrest and Detention**: Rawdon drove to Mr. Moss's mansion in Cursitor Street, Chancery Lane, and was inducted into that dismal place of hospitality. A little pink-eyed Jew-boy let the party in. Rawdon welcomed to ground-floor apartments by Mr. Moss.

**Prior History**: Colonel had been lodger at Mr. Moss's establishment once or twice before. On first visit as bachelor, liberated by generosity of his aunt. On second mishap, little Becky borrowed sum from Lord Southdown and coaxed her husband's creditor (who was her shawl, velvet-gown, lace pocket-handkerchief, trinket, and gim-crack purveyor) to take portion of sum claimed and Rawdon's promissory note for remainder.

**Current Predicament**: Colonel not so depressed as some mortals would be finding themselves barred into spunging-house; had been lodger here before. Reader may be assured such trivial domestic incidents can't infrequently occur in life of man who lives on nothing a year.

**Mr. Moss's Hospitality**: Offered Colonel his old bed. Recently slept in by Honorable Captain Famish of Fiftieth Dragoons, whose Ma took him out after fortnight but he punished champagne and had party every night—tip-top swells from clubs and West End, including Captain Ragg, Honorable Deuceace (Temple resident). Moss has Doctor of Divinity upstairs, five gents in coffee-room, and Mrs. Moss has table-d'hôte at half-past five with cards or music afterwards.

**Rawdon's Letter from Spunging-House**: Debt to Nathan one-hundred-fifty, with costs one-hundred-seventy. Asks Rebecca to send desk and clothes. Has seventy in desk. Instructs her to drive to Nathan's—offer seventy-five down and ask him to renew—say he'll take wine. If Nathan won't stand it, take ticker and spare things to Balls—must have sum tonight. Won't do to let it stand over; tomorrow's Sunday; beds here not very clean; there may be other things out against him. Glad it isn't Rawdon's Saturday for coming home. God bless you.

**Waiting and Rebecca's Failure (Chapter 22)**: Rawdon sealed letter with wafer and dispatched messenger. Went into courtyard and smoked cigar with tolerably easy mind. Calculated three hours utmost time before Becky should arrive and open his prison doors. Passed hours pretty cheerfully smoking, reading paper, and in coffee-room with Captain Walker, cutting for sixpences with pretty equal luck.

**Day Passed Away; No Becky (Chapter 22)**: The day passed and no messenger returned—no Becky. Mr. Moss's table-d'hôte was served at half-past five. Miss Moss (Miss Hem, as her papa called her) appeared without curl-papers; Mrs. Hem did honours of prime boiled leg of mutton and turnips. Rawdon ate with very faint appetite. Asked whether he would "stand" a bottle of champagne for company; he consented. Doorbell heard; young Moss answered; messenger returned with bag, desk and letter. Mrs. Moss gave him privacy to read. Letter was beautiful, highly scented, on pink paper with light green seal. (See Rebecca's Recent Letter above.)

**Rawdon's Reaction and Actions (Chapter 22)**: When Rawdon read letter, he turned red and looked savage; company at table easily perceived bad news reached him. All suppressed suspicions returned. She could not even sell trinkets to free him. She could laugh about compliments whilst he was in prison. Questions about who put him there; Wenham had walked with him. Could hardly bear to think of what he suspected. Left room hurriedly, opened desk, wrote two hurried lines directed to Sir Pitt or Lady Crawley, sent messenger to Gaunt Street by cab with promise of guinea if back in hour.

**Drinking and Waiting (Chapter 22)**: Went back to dining-room, called for more wine. Laughed and talked with strange boisterousness. Sometimes laughed madly at his own fears and went on drinking for hour, listening all the while for carriage which was to bring his fate back.

**Lady Jane's Rescue (Chapter 22)**: After some hours, voice at the door—timid, cheerful: "It is I, Rawdon...It is Jane." Rawdon quite overcome by that kind voice and presence. Ran up to her—caught her in his arms—gasped out inarticulate words of thanks and fairly sobbed on her shoulder. She did not know cause of his emotion. Bills of Mr. Moss quickly settled (perhaps to his disappointment, having counted on Colonel as guest over Sunday). Jane with beaming smiles and happiness in her eyes carried away Rawdon from bailiff's house in cab she had hastened in. "Pitt was gone to parliamentary dinner when Rawdon's note came, and so, dear Rawdon, I—I came myself"; she put kind hand in his. Perhaps it was well for Rawdon that Pitt was away. Rawdon thanked sister hundred times with ardour of gratitude which touched and almost alarmed that soft-hearted woman. Said in rude, artless way: "You—you don't know how I'm changed since I've known you, and—and little Rawdy. I—I'd like to change somehow. You see I want—I want—to be—" Did not finish; she could interpret it. That night after he left her, as she sat by her own little boy's bed, she prayed humbly for that poor way-worn sinner.

**Rawdon Comes Home (Chapter 22)**: Rawdon left her and walked home rapidly. It was nine o'clock at night. Ran across streets and great squares of Vanity Fair, came up breathless opposite his own house. Started back and fell against railings, trembling. Drawing-room windows blazing with light. She had said she was in bed and ill. Stood there some time, light from rooms on his pale face.

**DISCOVERY/CRISIS POINT**: Rawdon's suspicions crystallize upon finding Rebecca awake and entertaining in blazing drawing-room when she claimed illness prevented her coming to rescue him.

## Key Relationships (Chapter 22)

**Rawdon and Rebecca's Estrangement**: Estrangement more than he knew or acknowledged. She did not care; did not miss him. Looked upon him as errand-man and humble slave. Her letter reveals (or claims) distress about his imprisonment, yet she failed to rescue him despite having opportunities and visitors including Steyne.

**Rawdon and Lady Jane**: Very fond of young Rawdon, as was her little girl. Rawdon thankful for fondness. Best and honestest feelings of man came out in paternal feeling in their presence. Secured kindness and sincere regard. Jane's rescue of him, her kindness and compassion, deeply moves him and prompts reflection on his need for change.

## Minor Characters
- **Mr. Moss**: Proprietor of spunging-house on Cursitor Street; on very best of terms with Colonel
- **Miss Moss (Miss Hem)**: Dark-eyed damsel, daughter of Mr. Moss
- **Mrs. Moss**: Wife of Mr. Moss; hosts table-d'hôte at half-past five
- **Captain Walker**: Acquaintance of Rawdon at Moss's
- **Captain Famish**: Recent guest at Mr. Moss's, Fifth Dragoons (CORRECTION: Fiftieth Dragoons in prior text)
- **Nathan**: Money-lender; creditor for one-hundred-fifty debt (with costs one-hundred-seventy)
- **Mr. Blench**: Doctor who attended Rebecca, gave composing draught
- **Finette**: Rebecca's servant
- **Briggs, Old Mr. Osborne, Miss Osborne, Old Mr. Sedley, Mr. Wenham, Mr. Fiche, Messieurs de Truffigny and Champignac**: As previously documented
